analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax.
analysis.headline: The Fair Tax Act of 2009 was introduced in the Senate on January 22, 2009 with 5 Republican cosponsors, referred to the Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax, and replace them with a single national sales tax of 23% on nearly everything consumers buy. It would abolish the IRS by cutting off its funding after 2013 and have state governments collect the tax instead. To shield the poorest households, it would send every registered family a monthly cash rebate covering the tax on poverty-level spending. The sales tax would also die automatically if the constitutional amendment allowing the income tax were not repealed within seven years.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: the estate and gift tax disappears, and purchases made for investment purposes — buying stocks, real estate, or business assets — would be exempt from the sales tax entirely. Businesses also escape tax on everything they buy for business use. Families at or below the poverty line are protected by the monthly rebate, which returns the tax they would pay on poverty-level spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes, and imposes a national sales tax of 23% (tax-inclusive) starting in 2011.
Provides a monthly 'family consumption allowance' rebate to registered families equal to the sales tax on spending at the federal poverty level, cushioning the burden on low-income households.
Exempts all purchases for business, investment, or export purposes from the tax, so income earned from wealth would never pass through the tax at the point of saving.
Prohibits funding the IRS after fiscal year 2013 and replaces it with an Excise Tax Bureau and a Sales Tax Bureau, with states administering and collecting the sales tax for a 0.25% fee.
Sunsets the sales tax after seven years if the Sixteenth Amendment (authorizing the income tax) has not been repealed, conditioning the new system on a constitutional change.

analysis.who_pays: Households that spend most or all of their income — typical working and middle-class families — would pay the 23% tax on nearly every purchase, including rent and services, while the current income-based rates and credits they use would vanish. Because the stated 23% is measured against payments that include the tax, it comes to roughly 30 cents added to every dollar at the register. Social Security and Medicare would be funded from general sales tax revenue instead of dedicated payroll contributions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Families spending most of their income

drawbacks.text: The tax is levied at 23% of gross payments including the tax, which is arithmetically equivalent to about a 30% markup on shelf prices — far higher than any existing state sales tax.

Even with the poverty-level rebate, the tax falls on consumption while wealth-based income (investment purchases, large estates) is exempt, so the burden shifts toward households that live on wages and spend what they earn.

The bill repeals dedicated Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes and instead allocates sales tax revenue to those trust funds through annual appropriations, weakening the dedicated funding link for those benefits.
The system only holds if the Sixteenth Amendment is repealed; otherwise the sales tax sunsets, leaving the country to either go back to the old code or layer an income tax on top of the sales tax.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The appeal is real: filing income taxes would end, and the monthly rebate does genuinely shield households at or below the poverty line. But the design moves the tax burden off income from wealth — untaxed investment purchases and a repealed estate tax — and onto consumption, which is where working and middle-class families spend nearly everything they make. A family living paycheck to paycheck would pay the full rate on every dollar spent above the rebate; a wealthy household drawing down investments would pay almost nothing. The rebate softens the bottom of the distribution but does not change the overall tilt.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2009, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the entire two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Saxby Chambliss introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2009 in the Senate on January 22, 2009, joined by Senators Cornyn, Coburn, and Isakson.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; that referral was the last action of any kind the bill received.
Five senators, all Republicans, cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The bill never advanced out of the Finance Committee and received no floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working and middle-class households who pay tax on what they spend are better off that it never became law, since their consumption purchases would have carried the new 23% rate while investment purchases and large estates went untaxed. Supporters of the current income tax system also kept the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers who kept the current tax code

sides.party_line_note: All four introducing senators and all five cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it stayed in a Democratic-chaired committee until the Congress ended.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate and gift tax entirely and exempts investment purchases from the sales tax, so wealth passed to heirs and income from capital would never be taxed. The offsetting tax lands on consumption, which ordinary working families pay on nearly all their income.

All purchases made for investment purposes — securities, property held for appreciation — are explicitly untaxed, making wealth accumulation tax-free while wages are taxed at the cash register. The bill does tax fees for financial intermediation services, a partial counterweight.

Every registered seller must collect, report, and remit the 23% tax monthly and post bond if large, but sellers receive an administrative credit of the greater of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted as compensation. The compliance burden replaces the income tax compliance they shed.
States with existing sales taxes become the primary administrators of the federal tax, keeping a 0.25% fee on collections and a permanent new role in federal revenue administration.

With the income tax repealed and the IRS defunded after 2013, the industry built around income tax filing, planning, and disputes loses most of its market — the same simplification the bill's supporters cite as a public benefit.
